Lots of people in the comments keep saying to never use big negative letter spacing. I disagree. This is what I use with Geist:

16px → 0%
36px → -3%
100px+ → -5 to -6%

The “never go negative” rule is for body text. At 100px+ the default spacing looks loose, because the gaps between letters scale up with the size. Tightening them is what makes big headlines look clean.

Body text stays at 0%. The bigger the text, the tighter it gets. Nothing goes past -6%, because past that the letters start touching.

one mindset shift took me from charging $1000-$2000 per project to closing $ 50k+ deals:

I used to think $2,000 for a landing page was a lot. then I did the math.

a single full time designer, not accounting for development, animation, or anything else, just one designer, costs more than that per week.

that one realization changed everything.

suddenly $30,000 for a full project didn't feel expensive. it felt reasonable.

because when you break down what actually goes into delivering world-class work, the numbers start making a lot of sense.

as an agency you're not just paying for the person doing the design. you're paying for project managers, ops, sales, account management. people who have nothing to do with delivery but are essential to running the business.

when you factor all of that in, a $20,000/month retainer doesn't feel like a lot anymore. it's actually tight.
and when people hear $100k project, they imagine a one week sprint. it's not. it's usually a $15k/month retainer running across multiple months with a full team behind it.

spread out like that, it's incredibly reasonable for what's being delivered.

this mindset shift is what allowed us to start quoting bigger numbers with confidence and actually close those deals.

if you're still feeling uncomfortable quoting $10k, $20k, $100k projects, do the math on what it actually costs to deliver them properly.

the discomfort disappears pretty fast.

a lot of designers have been DMing me recently saying they're barely surviving in 2026.

designers who were killing it just a year or two ago. consistent clients, healthy revenue, everything going well. and now suddenly struggling to close anything.

here's what I think is happening.

the mid market is dying. the $2k-$10k project range is drying up fast.

all the money startups used to spend in the middle of the market is shifting. it's going either to the bottom end or the top end. nothing in between.

the ones going cheap, $200-$1,000, just want a slight improvement on whatever AI spat out. good enough, fast, cheap. they don't need a real designer for that.

then there's the other end. founders and companies at a later stage who want the real thing. $20k-$30k+ for a world class brand, product, or website that actually moves the needle. they're still spending. they're spending more than ever.

the in-between is disappearing.

if you're a designer stuck in the middle right now, the market is telling you something. either go premium and build the kind of portfolio that justifies $20k+ projects, or find a way to serve the bottom of the market at volume.

there's no comfortable middle ground left.

our step-by-step logo design process at http://kargul.studio. 🔖

for us, the logo is the most important part of the brand identity.

we start with research into the business, competitors and visual landscape, then usually present 3 to 5 genuinely different concepts every few days. we get feedback, learn what’s working and keep exploring from there.

sometimes it takes 5 concepts, sometimes 10, sometimes 20+. there’s no fixed cap because the logo is usually the most recognisable and long-lasting asset in the brand.

once the direction is right, we refine the geometry, spacing, proportions and optical balance, test it across sizes, monochrome versions, lockups and different typography pairings.

then we build the full brand around it: colour system, typography, layouts, imagery, applications, templates and the wider design system so everything works consistently across product, web, social and print.

8. Online Brand Guidelines and Delivery

The finished identity is delivered as an online brand guidelines system we build for each client. We prefer this to a static PDF because it's easier to navigate, share and keep up to date, and it gives the client a single place to reach the whole brand whenever they need it. It's also where everything lives:

- Brand strategy, logo files and usage rules
- Vector logos with PNG and SVG exports
- Light and dark, horizontal and vertical versions
- Icons and favicons, spacing and sizing
- Colour values, typography and layouts
- Application examples, templates and downloadable assets
- Iconography, image direction, tone of voice and social resources

It's built to be genuinely usable, and it can be shared with employees, developers, designers, agencies and future collaborators. It becomes the single source of truth for the brand and keeps growing alongside the company, so the identity can be put to work straight away across websites, products, marketing and future design work.

None of this is rigid. Some brands land on the final direction quickly, others need more exploration and testing, but the goal never changes, a distinctive, practical and memorable identity the client is proud of, and one that can grow with the business.

7. Final Refinement

Before delivery we step back and review the whole identity as one system, making sure the logo, typography, colours and applications all sit together. We push it across sizes, formats and backgrounds, from small digital sizes to large-scale use, light and dark, black and white, social avatars, website navigation, mobile interfaces and presentations. Any last technical or visual issues get fixed here, before anything ships.

6. Brand Applications

With the core identity defined, we start putting it to work on real assets, and this is where the brand really starts to feel complete. Depending on the project that can mean website sections and landing pages, social posts and profile images, app icons, email layouts, advertising, presentation slides, packaging, product screens, merchandise or stationery. Building these out shows the client how the system behaves in practice and surfaces anything that still needs adjusting, so we keep refining the typography, colour, spacing and layout until it all feels connected.

5. Colour System

Next comes the colour palette. We explore several directions and show the client how each one shifts the overall feeling of the brand, and we check them against the wider industry so the result doesn't land too close to a competitor or feel predictable for the market. A finished system usually covers primary and secondary colours, neutrals, backgrounds, text colours and accents, with accessibility and contrast built in so it holds up across digital products and marketing. As with everything else, we test the colours in real applications rather than signing off on them in isolation.

4. Typography

With the logo direction approved, we move on to the typography system. We look for typefaces that carry the brand's personality and hold up across everything it needs to do, from headlines and body text to interfaces, presentations and marketing. We test the type across website layouts, social posts, product screens, oversized headlines and small captions, aiming for something distinctive that's still practical, readable and easy for the client to use day to day.

3. Feedback and Logo Development

Once the first concepts are in front of the client, we dig into the feedback: what they connect with, what feels off, and which parts of each direction have the most potential. Sometimes one concept is clearly the winner. Other times the final direction comes from combining the strongest parts of several explorations.

From there we keep refining. A project might run through a handful of directions or more than 20, depending on how much experimentation it needs, and we don't stop until the client feels they've found the right logo. The logo is the most important and recognisable asset of the whole brand, so it earns the attention.

That work usually covers:

- Symbol, letterforms, spacing, proportions and geometry
- Balance, readability and small-size performance
- App icon versions and horizontal and vertical lockups
- Monochrome versions and the ways the mark has to adapt across formats

Everything gets tested in real environments, not just on the presentation slide.

2. Initial Logo Concepts

Within the first few days we usually prepare around 3 initial logo concepts. Each one takes a genuinely different direction rather than small variations on the same idea, which gives the client real options and helps us see which route feels closest to the brand.

We never present a logo cold. Each concept comes with the thinking behind it, how it connects to the company and how it could work as part of a larger identity. When it helps, we also show the concepts in realistic settings, things like website headers, app icons, social profiles, product screens, packaging, business cards, signage or merchandise. Seeing a mark live as a real brand is far more useful than judging it in isolation on a blank page.
